claim: Gastrulation modes range from stochastic translocation of individual cells to coordinated infolding of an epithelial sheet.
source: Modes of gastrulation range from stochastic translocation of individual cells to coordinated infolding of an epithelial sheet.
evidence: This is a general statement about gastrulation diversity presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: folded gastrulation and t48 are expressed and required for mesoderm invagination in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Both genes are expressed and required for mesoderm invagination in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster but do not appear during mesoderm ingression of the midge Chironomus riparius.
evidence: The manuscript presents expression data (Figure 3) and functional data (Figure 5) showing these genes are expressed and required in D. melanogaster.

claim: folded gastrulation and t48 do not appear during mesoderm ingression of Chironomus riparius.
source: Both genes are expressed and required for mesoderm invagination in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster but do not appear during mesoderm ingression of the midge Chironomus riparius.
evidence: The manuscript presents expression data showing Cri-fog1 and Cri-t48 are not detected until after mesoderm internalization is completed (Figure 3K,K',M,M').

claim: Early expression of either or both fog and t48 in C. riparius is sufficient to invoke mesoderm invagination similar to D. melanogaster.
source: We demonstrate that early expression of either or both of these genes in C.riparius is sufficient to invoke mesoderm invagination similar to D.melanogaster.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from mRNA injection experiments showing induced invagination (Figure 5B-D).

claim: The evolutionary transition from ingression to invagination is associated with a measurable increase in developmental robustness.
source: The possible genetic simplicity and a measurable increase in developmental robustness might explain repeated evolution of similar transitions in animal gastrulation.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data showing decreased variation in gastrulation after fog/t48 expression (Figure 6B,C).

claim: Changes in morphogenesis can originate from modifications of molecular patterning.
source: Such changes in morphogenesis can originate from modifications of molecular patterning, by adjusting the interpretation and integration of molecular patterning within and between cells, or by altering the translation of cellular decisions into changes of cytoskeleton and cell behavior, either alone or in combination (Davies, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Davies, 2013.

claim: The evolutionary gain or loss of gene activity has been shown to be a major source of morphological innovation.
source: The evolutionary gain or loss of gene activity has been shown to be a major source of morphological innovation, in particular between closely related species and in systems where patterns of gene expression correspond to a direct phenotypic output like insect wing and body pigmentation (Arnoult et al., 2013; Gompel et al., 2005; Prud'homme et al., 2006; Wittkopp et al., 2002a, 2002b).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster and Chironomus riparius shared their last common ancestor about 250 million years ago.
source: To address these questions, we have studied gastrulation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster and the midge Chironomus riparius, two fly species that shared their last common ancestor about 250 million years ago (Wiegmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wiegmann et al., 2011.

claim: The evolutionary history of D. melanogaster and C. riparius is characterized by an evolutionary transition between mesoderm invagination and mesoderm ingression.
source: Their evolutionary history is characterized by an evolutionary transition between two distinct modes of cell internalization during gastrulation, i.e. mesoderm invagination in D. melanogaster and mesoderm ingression in C. riparius (Figure 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Similar transitions between distinct modes of cell internalization have been observed repeatedly during the evolution of metazoan gastrulation.
source: Similar transitions between distinct modes of cell internalization have been observed repeatedly and in either direction during the evolution of metazoan gastrulation (Leptin, 2005; Nielsen, 2012; Solnica-Krezel and Sepich, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm invagination in flies constitutes a derived morphogenetic process that evolved from stochastic migration of individual cells.
source: In insects, the extremely fast and coordinated invagination of mesoderm cells constitutes a derived morphogenetic process that evolved from stochastic migration of individual cells (Johannsen and Butt, 1941; Roth, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm invagination in flies has been studied extensively in D. melanogaster.
source: Mesoderm invagination in flies has been studied extensively in D.melanogaster and thus provides an excellent reference system (Leptin, 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leptin, 2005.

claim: Mesoderm ingression has been previously reported for C. riparius as well as other species representing the most basal branches of flies.
source: mesoderm ingression is less well understood but has been previously reported for C.riparius as well as other species representing the most basal branches of flies (Goltsev et al., 2007; Ritter, 1890).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. riparius, mesodermal cells cluster on top of a shallow groove along the ventral midline during mesoderm internalization.
source: In transversal sections of C.riparius embryos that were about halfway through internalization, mesodermal cells clustered on top of a shallow groove along the ventral midline, while at a comparable stage in D.melanogaster they formed part of a deep ventral furrow (Figure 1A,B,F).
evidence: This statement is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In D. melanogaster, mesodermal cells form part of a deep ventral furrow at a comparable stage to C. riparius mesoderm internalization.
source: In transversal sections of C.riparius embryos that were about halfway through internalization, mesodermal cells clustered on top of a shallow groove along the ventral midline, while at a comparable stage in D.melanogaster they formed part of a deep ventral furrow (Figure 1A,B,F).
evidence: This statement is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The position of mesoderm cells during progression of mesoderm formation can be approximated by their nuclei in both C. riparius and D. melanogaster.
source: In both species, we found that the position of mesoderm cells during progression of mesoderm formation could be approximated by their nuclei (Figure 1E,E').
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E,E'.

claim: Relative to the onset of germband extension, mesoderm internalization starts and ends earlier in D. melanogaster than in C. riparius.
source: We found that relative to the onset of germband extension, mesoderm internalization started and ended earlier in D.melanogaster than in C.riparius (Figure 1F).
evidence: This statement is supported by developmental staging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Mesoderm cell behavior varies substantially along the anterior-to-posterior axis in individual embryos.
source: Notably, when we used cell position in transversal sections to assess the coherence of mesoderm cell behavior in individual embryos (see Materials and methods), we found mesoderm cell behavior to vary substantially along the anterior-to-posterior axis (Figure 2A–B'').
evidence: This statement is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2A-B''.

claim: Variation in mesoderm cell behavior along the anterior-to-posterior axis is more pronounced in C. riparius embryos than in D. melanogaster.
source: These differences were more pronounced in C.riparius embryos than in D.melanogaster and indicated that the classification of cell internalization in fixed embryos as either ingressive or invaginative could not be based on qualitative measures of transversal sections alone.
evidence: This statement is based on observations from Figure 2A-B'' comparing the two species.

claim: Mitosis was rarely detected in either C. riparius or D. melanogaster during mesoderm internalization.
source: While mitosis was rarely detected in either species during mesoderm internalization, wild-type embryos of C.riparius and D.melanogaster exhibited significant divergence in all other parameters (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Wild-type embryos of C. riparius and D. melanogaster exhibit significant divergence in morphological parameters of mesoderm formation.
source: While mitosis was rarely detected in either species during mesoderm internalization, wild-type embryos of C.riparius and D.melanogaster exhibited significant divergence in all other parameters (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Three principal parameters permit the best discrimination between ingression and invagination: cell internalization, the depth of the ventral furrow, and epithelial integrity.
source: We found three principal parameters that, regardless of intra-species variation in space and time, permitted the best discrimination between ingression and invagination: cell internalization, the depth of the ventral furrow and epithelial integrity (Figure 2F–F''').
evidence: This statement is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 2F-F'''.

claim: Invagination in D. melanogaster is characterized by high tissue integrity, a deep ventral furrow, and a high number of internalized cells.
source: Accordingly, invagination in D.melanogaster was characterized by high tissue integrity, a deep ventral furrow, and a high number of internalized cells, while ingression in C.riparius was characterized by low tissue integrity, a shallow ventral furrow, and a lower number of internalized cells.
evidence: This statement is based on the principal component analysis results from Figure 2F-F'''.

claim: Ingression in C. riparius is characterized by low tissue integrity, a shallow ventral furrow, and a lower number of internalized cells.
source: Accordingly, invagination in D.melanogaster was characterized by high tissue integrity, a deep ventral furrow, and a high number of internalized cells, while ingression in C.riparius was characterized by low tissue integrity, a shallow ventral furrow, and a lower number of internalized cells.
evidence: This statement is based on the principal component analysis results from Figure 2F-F'''.

claim: In D. melanogaster, mesoderm internalization is orchestrated by two zygotic transcription factors, Twist and Snail.
source: In D.melanogaster, mesoderm internalization is orchestrated by two zygotic transcription factors, Twist (Twi) and Snail (Sna) (Leptin and Grunewald, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Twist and Snail are expressed along the ventral midline of the D. melanogaster embryo.
source: Both genes are expressed along the ventral midline of the embryo (Figure 3B–C')
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3B-C'.

claim: Twist and Snail instruct zygotic expression of fog, t48, and mist in D. melanogaster.
source: where they instruct zygotic expression of fog (Figure 3D,D'), t48 (Figure 3E,E'), and mist (Figure 3F,F')
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3D-F' and is consistent with known regulatory relationships.

claim: cta and RhoGEF2 are expressed ubiquitously in D. melanogaster embryos.
source: while cta and RhoGEF2 are expressed ubiquitously (Figure 3G–H') (Costa et al., 1994; Kölsch et al., 2007; Manning et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3G-H' and citations to previous literature.

claim: Orthologues of twi, sna, t48, RhoGEF2, fog, mist, and cta could be identified in C. riparius and in major families of winged insects.
source: Orthologues of twi and sna, t48, and RhoGEF2, along with genes encoding the GPCR ligand Fog, the receptor Mist, and the Gα subunit Cta, could be identified in C.riparius and in major families of winged insects where genome sequence data is available (Pterygota, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The conserved gene set of twi, sna, t48, RhoGEF2, fog, mist, and cta originated over 400 million years ago.
source: The universal conservation of this gene set demonstrates its evolutionary importance and suggests that it originated over 400 million years ago (Misof et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is based on phylogenetic inference supported by a citation to Misof et al., 2014.

claim: Cri-twi and Cri-sna are both expressed along the ventral midline of the C. riparius blastoderm embryo.
source: We found that Cri-twi and Cri-sna were both expressed along the ventral midline of the blastoderm embryo (Figure 3I–J').
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3I-J'.

claim: Knockdown of Cri-twi results in embryos that lack a visible ventral groove but still show some cell internalization.
source: The knockdown of Cri-twi by RNAi resulted in embryos that lacked a visible ventral groove. Despite the knockdown of Cri-twi, nuclei of internalized cells could still be observed within the ventral-most 10–15% of the embryonic circumference (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: This statement is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Knockdown of Cri-sna produces an abnormally thin ventral epithelium with spherical nuclei and a failure of proper mesoderm internalization.
source: The knockdown of Cri-sna produced an abnormally thin ventral epithelium with spherical nuclei and a failure of proper mesoderm internalization (Figure 4C).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Similar expression and phenotypes of twi and sna have been reported in experimental manipulations in D. melanogaster.
source: Similar expression and phenotypes have been reported in experimental manipulations of twi and sna in D.melanogaster (Leptin and Grunewald, 1990)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm cells in C. riparius and D. melanogaster receive and require essentially the same zygotic patterning information.
source: Similar expression and phenotypes have been reported in experimental manipulations of twi and sna in D.melanogaster (Leptin and Grunewald, 1990), indicating that mesoderm cells receive and require essentially the same zygotic patterning information in C.riparius and D.melanogaster.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the similarity of expression patterns and knockdown phenotypes between the two species.

claim: Cri-mist is expressed along the ventral midline and in the domain of Cri-twi expression.
source: Expression of Cri-mist along the ventral midline and in the domain of Cri-twi expression (Figure 3N,N')
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3N,N'.

claim: Cri-cta is expressed ubiquitously in C. riparius embryos.
source: as well as ubiquitous expression of Cri-cta (Figure 3O,O')
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3O,O'.

claim: Cri-RhoGEF2 is expressed ubiquitously in C. riparius embryos.
source: and Cri-RhoGEF2 (Figure 3P,P')
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3P,P'.

claim: In D. melanogaster, fog and t48 are initially subject to maternal loading.
source: In D.melanogaster, both molecules are initially subject to maternal loading (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (Costa et al., 1994; Strutt and White, 1994; Zusman and Wieschaus, 1985)
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citations to previous literature.

claim: In D. melanogaster, fog and t48 are later expressed zygotically along the ventral midline of blastoderm embryos in a Twist-dependent manner.
source: and are later expressed zygotically along the ventral midline of blastoderm embryos in a Twist-dependent manner (Costa et al., 1994; Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. riparius, Cri-fog1 and Cri-t48 transcripts are not detected until mesoderm internalization has been completed.
source: In C.riparius, Cri-fog1 and Cri-t48 transcripts were not detected until mesoderm internalization had been completed (Figure 3K,K',M,M', Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3K,K',M,M' and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cri-fog2 is expressed prior to mesoderm internalization in the central third of the C. riparius embryo, in a domain broader than that of Cri-twi expression.
source: A second fog orthologue, Cri-fog2, was expressed prior to mesoderm internalization in the central third of the embryo, in a domain broader than that seen for the expression of Cri-twi (Figure 3L,L').
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3L,L'.

claim: The GPCR ligand Cri-Fog2 and its receptor Cri-Mist may not play the same prominent role in C. riparius mesoderm formation as they do in D. melanogaster.
source: This suggested that the GPCR ligand it encodes and, by extension, its receptor Cri-Mist, may not play the same prominent role in C.riparius mesoderm formation as they do in D.melanogaster.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the expression pattern of Cri-fog2 being broader than Cri-twi.

claim: Knockdown of Cri-mist results in small but significant differences in median cell internalization and furrow depth compared to water-injected embryos.
source: Following the quantitative analysis, we found that the median cell internalization and furrow depth differed in Cri-mist RNAi embryos from water injected embryos (Figure 4D).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Knockdown of Cri-fog2 results in a small but significant increase in furrow and maximal cell depth.
source: In Cri-fog2 RNAi embryos, the difference was smaller and significant only for an increase in the furrow and maximal cell depth (Figure 4E).
evidence: This statement is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: All effects after Cri-mist and Cri-fog2 knockdown are substantially smaller than in Cri-twi and Cri-sna RNAi embryos.
source: All effects after Cri-mist and Cri-fog2 knockdown were substantially smaller than in Cri-twi and Cri-sna RNAi embryos and close to the sensitivity of our method (<10% of nuclear size)
evidence: This statement is based on comparison of quantitative data from Figures 4C-E.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of fog and t48 in C. riparius embryos induces an invagination of the mesoderm.
source: In response to this unspecific and early ubiquitous expression of fog and t48, C.riparius embryos exhibited an invagination of the mesoderm.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from mRNA injection experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ubiquitous expression of fog and t48 in C. riparius results in the formation of a distinct continuous ventral furrow, qualitatively comparable to that of D. melanogaster.
source: First, we observed the formation of a distinct continuous ventral furrow, qualitatively comparable to that of D.melanogaster (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Induced invagination in C. riparius embryos is characterized by increased epithelial integrity and an increased furrow depth.
source: Then in particular, the induced invagination in C.riparius embryos was characterized by increased epithelial integrity and an increased furrow depth (Figure 5B).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Early ubiquitous expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48 induces mesoderm invagination in C. riparius that resembles that seen with D. melanogaster fog and t48.
source: Following early ubiquitous expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48, C.riparius embryos responded with an invagination of the mesoderm which resembled that seen with the D.melanogaster forms of fog and t48 (Figure 5C)
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A gain of early ubiquitous expression of fog or t48 is sufficient for the induction of mesoderm invagination in C. riparius.
source: suggesting that a gain of early ubiquitous expression of one or both of these molecules was sufficient for the induction of mesoderm invagination.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental results showing that either Cri-fog or Cri-t48 alone can induce invagination.

claim: Early ubiquitous expression of either Cri-fog or Cri-t48 alone is sufficient to induce invagination in C. riparius.
source: Upon early ubiquitous expression of either Cri-fog or Cri-t48 alone, C.riparius embryos displayed induced furrows overall, with increased epithelial integrity and deeper internalization very similar to the features observed in Cri-fog and Cri-t48 double-injected embryos (Figure 5D).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Cells in embryos expressing Cri-fog appear less variable in behavior than in embryos expressing Cri-t48.
source: Differences were noted in the behavior of cells within individual embryos: these appeared less variable in embryos expressing Cri-fog than in embryos expressing Cri-t48 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: fog and t48 operate differently in transmitting instructions to the cytoskeleton.
source: Our results indicate that fog and t48 operate differently in transmitting instructions to the cytoskeleton
evidence: This statement is inferred from the observation that Cri-fog and Cri-t48 show different levels of variability when expressed individually.

claim: Gaining early expression of either fog or t48 alone is sufficient to invoke a change in the mode of mesoderm internalization.
source: while at the same time demonstrating that gaining early expression of either gene alone was sufficient to invoke a change in the mode of mesoderm internalization.
evidence: This statement is based on experimental data showing that either gene alone can induce invagination (Figure 5D).

claim: Loss of either fog or t48 activity in the mesoderm alone affects ventral furrow formation in D. melanogaster but does not block it.
source: While the loss of either fog or t48 activity in the mesoderm alone affects ventral furrow formation, it does not block it (Costa et al., 1994; Kölsch et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Combined knockdown of fog and t48 functions in the ventral blastoderm of D. melanogaster abolishes ventral furrow formation and results in ingression-like mesoderm cell behavior reminiscent of C. riparius wildtype development.
source: but the combined knockdown of fog and t48 functions in the ventral blastoderm abolished ventral furrow formation and resulted in ingression-like mesoderm cell behavior reminiscent of C.riparius wildtype development (Figure 5E).
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Expression of either Cri-fog or Cri-t48 is sufficient for a morphogenetic response that appears indistinguishable from the expression of both genes together.
source: Our observations in C.riparius suggested that expression of either Cri-fog or Cri-t48 was already sufficient for a morphogenetic response that appeared indistinguishable from the expression of both genes together.
evidence: This statement is based on experimental data from Figure 5D showing similar effects of single and double injections.

claim: A coherent epithelium provides increased mechanical stability compared to individual cells.
source: In comparison with individual cells, a coherent epithelium provides increased mechanical stability (Lecuit and Lenne, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Following induced expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48, there is an overall decrease in the variability of phenotypes in C. riparius embryos.
source: Following the induced expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48, we observed an overall decrease in the variability of phenotypes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The decrease in variability of measured features after Cri-fog and Cri-t48 expression is observed within embryos.
source: The decrease in the variability of the measured features was observed within embryos (Figure 6C)
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The decrease in variability within embryos may reflect the increase in cell coordination due to the induced change in the mode of gastrulation.
source: and may reflect the increase in cell coordination due to the induced change in the mode of gastrulation.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in variability.

claim: A decrease in variability is also detected between embryos after Cri-fog and Cri-t48 expression.
source: Consistent with conceptual consideration of robustness (Félix and Barkoulas, 2015), we detected a decrease in variability also between embryos (Figure 6C)
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C and a citation to previous literature on robustness.

claim: C. riparius embryonic development becomes more robust against cellular mechanical perturbations after Cri-fog and Cri-t48 expression.
source: which indicated that C.riparius embryonic development became more robust against cellular mechanical perturbations.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the observed decrease in variability between embryos.

claim: Expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48 significantly increases the number of cells that are internalized immediately after the onset of germband extension.
source: Following the expression of Cri-fog and Cri-t48, we found a significant increase in the number of cells that were internalized (Figure 6D).
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: After 48 hours, twitching and moving is observed in embryos injected with Cri-fog and Cri-t48 at a frequency similar to control-injected embryos.
source: An increased robustness against mechanical perturbation and developmental efficiency did not appear to trigger conflicts with subsequent embryonic muscle formation and enervation: after 48 hr, twitching and moving was observed in embryos injected with Cri-fog and Cri-t48 at a frequency (40%; n=500) similar to control-injected embryos (44%; n=531).
evidence: This statement is supported by observational data on embryo viability.

claim: Mesoderm invagination induced by fog and t48 is associated with a measurable increase in the robustness and efficiency of gastrulation.
source: Our results thus indicate that, beyond a simple coordination of cell behavior, mesoderm invagination induced by fog and t48 is associated with a measurable increase in the robustness and efficiency of gastrulation.
evidence: This statement is based on the quantitative data from Figure 6 showing decreased variability and increased internalization.

claim: The increased robustness and efficiency of mesoderm invagination could have provided an adaptive advantage in specific environments and contexts encountered by the predecessors of D. melanogaster.
source: Given the simplicity of the system and the extent of its fixation over long periods of evolutionary time, such traits could have provided an adaptive advantage in specific environments and contexts encountered by the predecessors of D.melanogaster after divergence from the last common ancestor shared with C.riparius.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary advantages.

claim: Mesoderm ingression in C. riparius correlates at the genetic level with the absence of significant fog and t48 activity in the early embryo.
source: Our analysis of C.riparius mesoderm morphogenesis has allowed us to associate two distinct modes of mesoderm internalization with specific differences in developmental gene expression. We could demonstrate that mesoderm ingression in C.riparius correlates at the genetic level with the absence of significant fog and t48 activity in the early embryo.
evidence: This statement is based on the expression data showing lack of early fog and t48 expression in C. riparius (Figure 3).

claim: An evolutionary gain of early fog and t48 activity may constitute a genetic switch to change the mode of fly gastrulation.
source: In comparison with mesoderm invagination in D.melanogaster, these results suggested that an evolutionary gain of early fog and t48 activity may constitute a genetic switch to change the mode of fly gastrulation.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation based on the comparative expression and functional data.

claim: The activities of either fog or t48 alone or both genes together are sufficient to invoke a Drosophila-like invagination of the mesoderm in C. riparius embryos.
source: We functionally tested this hypothesis by early ubiquitous expression of fog and t48 in C.riparius embryos, and we found that the activities of either gene alone or both genes together were sufficient to invoke a Drosophila-like invagination of the mesoderm in C.riparius embryos.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data from Figure 5B-D.

claim: Mesoderm invagination in C. riparius increases developmental robustness and efficiency.
source: Our data suggest that mesoderm invagination in C.riparius increases developmental robustness and efficiency.
evidence: This statement is supported by quantitative data from Figure 6.

claim: Invagination preserves the epithelial character of the mesoderm during internalization and thus decouples epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in the mesoderm from the positional cell exchange during germband extension.
source: Additionally, invagination preserves the epithelial character of the mesoderm during internalization and thus decouples epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in the mesoderm from the positional cell exchange during germband extension.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation about the developmental consequences of invagination.

claim: Invagination could have facilitated the use of positional information of pre-gastrulation blastoderm patterning for post-gastrulation differentiation of the internalized mesoderm.
source: As a result, the anterior-to-posterior order of mesoderm cells may be more effectively preserved throughout gastrulation. During the course of evolution, this could have facilitated the use of positional information of pre-gastrulation blastoderm patterning for post-gastrulation differentiation of the internalized mesoderm.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary consequences.

claim: Unspecific injection of fog and t48 mRNA has a specific effect on C. riparius mesoderm internalization instead of leading to pleiotropic morphogenetic defects.
source: Unspecific injection of fog and t48 mRNA, which at best corresponds to a strong maternal loading, had a specific effect on C.riparius mesoderm internalization instead of leading to pleiotropic morphogenetic defects (Figure 5).
evidence: This statement is based on experimental observations from Figure 5.

claim: For C. riparius embryos to respond to early ubiquitous expression of fog or t48 in a spatially restricted manner along the ventral midline, the activity of either gene must be realized differently in different regions of the blastoderm embryo.
source: In order for C.riparius embryos to respond to the early ubiquitous expression of fog or t48 in a spatially restricted manner along the ventral midline, the activity of either gene was apparently realized differently in different regions of the C.riparius blastoderm embryo.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the observation that ubiquitous expression leads to ventral-specific effects.

claim: A strong and exclusively ventral response to fog and t48 activity in C. riparius could explain a local change in the mode of morphogenesis despite ubiquitous gene expression.
source: A strong and exclusively ventral response to fog and t48 activity in C.riparius could explain such a local change in the mode of morphogenesis in spite of ubiquitous gene expression.
evidence: This statement is a speculative explanation for the observed ventral-specific response.

claim: Ancestral modes of gastrulation can be built upon a gene repertoire that is in part distinct from the network known in D. melanogaster.
source: Recent work has shown that ancestral modes of gastrulation can be built upon a gene repertoire that is in part distinct from the network known in D.melanogaster (Pers et al., 2016; Stappert et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The local response to ubiquitous fog and t48 activity in C. riparius embryos may be elicited by an unknown fog/t48 sensitive pathway under control of twist and/or snail.
source: and the local response to ubiquitous fog and t48 activity in C.riparius embryos may thus be elicited by an unknown fog/t48 sensitive pathway under control of twist and/or snail.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism of ventral-specific response.

claim: Ectopic fog and t48 in C. riparius may act through a conserved genetic cascade present also in D. melanogaster.
source: Alternatively, ectopic fog and t48 in C.riparius act through a conserved genetic cascade present also in D.melanogaster.
evidence: This statement is a speculative alternative hypothesis.

claim: If ectopic fog and t48 act through a conserved cascade, the activity of at least one component downstream of fog and t48 would have to be locally restricted to the ventral blastoderm.
source: In this case, the activity of at least one component of this pathway downstream of fog and t48 would have to be locally restricted to the ventral blastoderm.
evidence: This statement is a logical inference from the alternative hypothesis.

claim: Mist is a possible candidate for a conserved component with spatially restricted activity downstream of fog and t48.
source: A possible candidate for such a conserved component with spatially restricted activity downstream of fog and t48 is the G-protein coupled receptor Mist.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis based on the expression pattern of Mist.

claim: In embryos of both C. riparius and D. melanogaster, mist is expressed in a narrow domain along the ventral midline.
source: In embryos of both species, C.riparius and D.melanogaster, mist is expressed in a narrow domain along the ventral midline (Figure 3F,F',N,N').
evidence: This statement is supported by expression data shown in Figure 3F,F',N,N'.

claim: Mist transduces signaling of the extracellular ligand Fog to the intracellular receptor-coupled G-protein Gα12/13 Cta.
source: Mist transduces signaling of the extracellular ligand Fog to the intracellular receptor-coupled G-protein Gα12/13 Cta
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of the GPCR signaling pathway.

claim: During D. melanogaster mesoderm invagination, Mist signaling results in apical RhoGEF2 activation.
source: which during D.melanogaster mesoderm invagination results in apical RhoGEF2 activation.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge of the signaling pathway in D. melanogaster.

claim: RhoGEF2 is intracellularly enriched at the apical cell membrane by its transmembrane anchor T48.
source: RhoGEF2 is intracellularly enriched at the apical cell membrane by its transmembrane anchor T48
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Apical RhoGEF2 activation results in constriction of the apical actomyosin network and coordinated cell shape changes that lead to ventral invagination.
source: and apical RhoGEF2 activation subsequently results in constriction of the apical actomyosin network and thus coordinated cell shape changes that lead to ventral invagination (Kerridge et al., 2016; Manning et al., 2013; Parks and Wieschaus, 1991; Dawes-Hoang et al., 2005; Morize et al., 1998; Barrett et al., 1997; Häcker and Perrimon, 1998; Fox and Peifer, 2007; Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In blastoderm embryos of D. melanogaster, fog and mist are expressed in partially overlapping domains.
source: In blastoderm embryos of D.melanogaster, fog and mist are expressed in partially overlapping domains
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Tissue invagination in D. melanogaster is observed only where the expression of fog and mist coincides.
source: and tissue invagination is observed only where the expression of both genes coincides (Manning et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The activity of ectopic ubiquitous fog and t48 expression in C. riparius appears to be limited to a ventral domain that overlaps with endogenous Cri-mist expression.
source: Similarly, the activity of ectopic ubiquitous fog and t48 expression in C.riparius appears to be limited to a ventral domain that overlaps with endogenous Cri-mist expression.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the comparison with D. melanogaster and the expression pattern of Cri-mist.

claim: Mesoderm ingression as an ancestral mode of cell internalization is based on comparatively low-level RhoGEF2 activity.
source: Based on the expression of Cri-cta and Cri-mist and the induction of mesoderm invagination through ectopic fog and t48, we speculate that mesoderm ingression as an ancestral mode of cell internalization is based on comparatively low-level RhoGEF2 activity (Figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is a speculative model based on the experimental results.

claim: Low-level RhoGEF2 activity may be invoked by scattered expression of the ligand Fog or by low-frequency self-activation of Mist.
source: This low level of RhoGEF2 activity may be invoked by scattered expression of the ligand Fog, or, as has been suggested before, by low-frequency self-activation of Mist (Manning and Rogers, 2014).
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Under conditions of low RhoGEF2 activity, cells undergo an early epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and leave the blastoderm stochastically due to individual rather than collective cell shape changes.
source: Our results in wildtype C.riparius embryos suggest that under such conditions, cells undergo an early epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and leave the blastoderm stochastically due to individual rather than collective cell shape changes.
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation of the C. riparius wildtype phenotype.

claim: Cell behavior changes under conditions that increase RhoGEF2 activity at the apex of mesoderm cells.
source: This cell behavior changes under conditions that increase RhoGEF2 activity at the apex of mesoderm cells
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental results showing that fog and t48 expression changes cell behavior.

claim: Increased RhoGEF2 activity can be achieved non-cell-autonomously by increasing GPCR signaling strength through elevated levels of the secreted ligand Fog.
source: which may be achieved in two ways: either non-cell-autonomously, by increasing GPCR signaling strength through elevated levels of the secreted ligand Fog
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis about mechanisms of increasing RhoGEF2 activity.

claim: Increased RhoGEF2 activity can be achieved cell-autonomously by improving GPCR signaling efficiency through the apically enriched membrane anchor T48.
source: or cell-autonomously, by improving GPCR signaling efficiency through the apically enriched membrane anchor T48 (Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nature may have used similar changes during fly evolution that led to the highly efficient GPCR signaling in the ventral blastoderm of D. melanogaster.
source: It is tempting to speculate that nature used similar changes during fly evolution (Figure 7B), which ultimately led to the highly efficient GPCR signaling in the ventral blastoderm of D.melanogaster (Figure 7C).
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: C. riparius and D. melanogaster diverged from a last common ancestor about 250 million years ago.
source: Although C.riparius and D.melanogaster diverged from a last common ancestor about 250 million years ago (Wiegmann et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Surprisingly simple genetic changes are sufficient to reversibly switch between cell ingression and tissue invagination.
source: our functional analysis of mesoderm internalization in both species suggests that surprisingly simple genetic changes are sufficient to reversibly switch between cell ingression and tissue invagination.
evidence: This statement is inferred from the experimental results showing that single genes can induce the transition.

claim: Mesoderm formation in flies has evolved either from a Drosophila-like ancestor that lost early fog and t48 expression in C. riparius, or from a Chironomus-like ancestor that gained early fog and t48 expression leading to D. melanogaster.
source: Without an overt genetic directionality, mesoderm formation in flies has thus evolved either from a Drosophila-like ancestor that essentially lost maternal as well as zygotic fog and t48 expression in C.riparius, or from a Chironomus-like ancestor that gained early embryonic fog and t48 expression in successive steps leading to the developmental network described for D.melanogaster.
evidence: This statement presents two alternative evolutionary scenarios based on the comparative data.

claim: C. riparius may have diverged significantly from the last common ancestor of flies due to recent lineage-specific gene duplications.
source: We cannot exclude that C.riparius evolved from a Drosophila-like ancestor by a secondary loss of early fog and t48 expression, and recent lineage-specific gene duplications, resulting, e.g., in two fog copies or pangolin (Klomp et al., 2015), suggest that C.riparius may have diverged significantly from the last common ancestor of flies.
evidence: This statement is a speculative consideration supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: C. riparius rather than D. melanogaster is more reminiscent of ancestral mesoderm internalization in flies.
source: Overall however, we favor the hypothesis that C.riparius rather than D.melanogaster is more reminiscent of ancestral mesoderm internalization in flies.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis favored by the authors.

claim: Mesoderm ingression has been reported for Anopheles gambiae, an independent family at the base of Diptera.
source: Supporting this view, mesoderm ingression has been reported for an independent family at the base of the insect order of flies (Diptera), A.gambiae (Goltsev et al., 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm ingression has been reported in the beetle Tribolium castaneum.
source: in the beetle Tribolium castaneum (Handel et al., 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm formation in insects evolved from an ancestor with an ingression-like mode of cell internalization.
source: and reflects the general view that mesoderm formation in insects evolved from an ancestor with an ingression-like mode of cell internalization (Roth, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The evolutionary origin of the D. melanogaster gene network is linked to the gain of a ubiquitous maternal and a ventral zygotic enhancer for fog and t48.
source: Experimental induction of mesoderm invagination by early fog or t48 expression in C.riparius embryos suggests that the evolutionary origin of the D.melanogaster gene network is linked to the gain of a ubiquitous maternal and a ventral zygotic enhancer for fog and t48.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental results.

claim: High levels of maternal-like ubiquitous expression of fog and t48 are sufficient to invoke mesoderm invagination in C. riparius.
source: Our results in C.riparius suggest that high levels of maternal-like ubiquitous expression of fog and t48 are sufficient to invoke mesoderm invagination.
evidence: This statement is based on experimental results from mRNA injection experiments.

claim: Both fog and t48 are expressed ubiquitously in pre-blastoderm embryos of D. melanogaster.
source: Consistent with a critical role of maternal fog and t48 in the evolutionary origin of mesoderm invagination, both genes are also expressed ubiquitously in pre-blastoderm embryos of D.melanogaster (Costa et al., 1994; Strutt and White, 1994) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and expression data.

claim: Only a weak maternal contribution has been functionally demonstrated for fog in D. melanogaster.
source: However, so far only a weak maternal contribution has been functionally demonstrated for fog (Zusman and Wieschaus, 1985)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The main function of fog and t48 in D. melanogaster mesoderm invagination is derived from their zygotic, twist-dependent ventral expression.
source: and the main function of both genes in D.melanogaster mesoderm invagination is derived from their zygotic, twist-dependent ventral expression (Costa et al., 1994; Kölsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mesoderm invagination in D. melanogaster originated either by the origin of Twist-dependent enhancers in fog or t48 followed by gain of maternal expression, or vice versa.
source: Thus, mesoderm invagination in D.melanogaster originated by the origin of highly specific Twist-dependent enhancers in fog or t48 and later the gain of maternal expression in both genes, or vice versa.
evidence: This statement presents two alternative evolutionary scenarios.

claim: The authors favor the idea that the origin of mesoderm invagination was built on the gain of a maternal enhancer.
source: We favor the idea that the origin of mesoderm invagination was built on the gain of a maternal enhancer, which may evolve more likely de novo from random sequence turnover.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis favored by the authors.

claim: fog and t48 may have acquired their role in coordinating cell behavior during epithelial morphogenesis coincidentally with the evolution of fly gastrulation.
source: fog and t48 may have acquired their role in coordinating cell behavior during epithelial morphogenesis coincedently with the evolution of fly gastrulation.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: In D. melanogaster, the functions of fog, mist, and RhoGEF2 are not limited to gastrulation but are also implicated in wing, leg, and salivary gland morphogenesis.
source: However, in D.melanogaster, the functions of fog, mist, and RhoGEF2 do not appear to be limited to gastrulation; the genes have been additionally implicated in gastrulation-like folding of epithelia during wing, leg, and salivary gland morphogenesis (Manning et al., 2013; Nikolaidou and Barrett, 2004; Ratnaparkhi and Zinn, 2007)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of fog and t48 orthologues in insect genomes overlaps with the phylogenetic occurrence of winged appendages and salivary glands.
source: and the presence of fog and t48 orthologues in insect genomes overlaps with the phylogenetic occurrence of winged appendages and salivary glands (Krenn and Aspöck, 2012) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and phylogenetic data.

claim: fog and t48 have played a role in epithelial morphogenesis during late stages of development long before the origin of mesoderm invagination.
source: We therefore favor a model in which fog and t48 have played a role in epithelial morphogenesis, at least during late stages of development, long before the origin of mesoderm invagination.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis favored by the authors.

claim: fog and t48 were subsequently recruited for a function in modern, Drosophila-like gastrulation with a delayed epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
source: Both genes were then subsequently recruited for a function in modern, Drosophila-like gastrulation with a delayed epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis about evolutionary recruitment.

claim: Such recruitments of fog and t48 may occur independently and repeatedly.
source: Such recruitments may occur independently and repeatedly
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: It will be informative to study a possible role of fog and t48 in hymenopterans.
source: and it will be informative to study a possible role of fog and t48 in hymenopterans.
evidence: This statement is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Species in the hymenopteran order internalize their mesoderm in a coordinated way as a stiff, coherent plate along the ventral midline.
source: Species in this insect order also internalize their mesoderm in a coordinated way, but as a stiff, coherent plate along the ventral midline (Fleig and Sander, 1988; Roth, 2004; Sauer, 1954).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recruiting genes with roles in later developmental stages into the maternal germline may provide the missing link between divergence in late development and diversity that appears earlier.
source: Recruiting genes with roles in later developmental stages into the maternal germline may provide the missing link between the divergence seen in late phases of a species' development with diversity that appears earlier – often referred to as a developmental 'hour glass' (Duboule, 1994; Raff, 1996; Kalinka and Tomancak, 2012).
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature on the developmental hourglass concept.

claim: Maternal recruitment provides a simple, and possibly non-gradual, evolutionary path toward altering early embryonic stages prior to the onset of zygotic transcription.
source: This provides a simple, and possibly non-gradual, evolutionary path toward altering early embryonic stages prior to the onset of zygotic transcription
evidence: This statement is a speculative interpretation about evolutionary mechanisms.

claim: Maternal recruitment may reflect a more general mechanism that facilitated the diversification of early embryonic development.
source: and it may reflect a more general mechanism that facilitated the diversification of early embryonic development.
evidence: This statement is a speculative hypothesis about general evolutionary mechanisms.
